hypothesis: If Darwin's figure holds, the late Chalk (latest Secondary/Mesozoic) is dated at about 300 million years or more before present, and the time since then is at least 270 Myr.
pass_criterion: The International Chronostratigraphic Chart gives a numeric age for the top of the Cretaceous (Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, end of the Chalk) of at least 270 Ma. The same applies if the base of the Upper Cretaceous, which is the earliest possible Chalk age, is at least 270 Ma. That would support 'roughly 300 million years or more'.
fail_criterion: The age of the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary is below 270 Ma, and the base of the Upper Cretaceous, which is the oldest age for the Chalk, is also below 270 Ma. Then the claim that about 300 Myr or more have elapsed since the late Secondary is refuted. A boundary age near 66 Ma would make Darwin's figure roughly 4.5 times too large.
interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' is mapped to the Late Cretaceous, the Chalk Group (Upper Cretaceous), and the end of the Secondary/Mesozoic is mapped to the K–Pg boundary. 'Years elapsed since' is mapped to the numeric age in Ma of that boundary, read from the chart. This test checks the elapsed-time conclusion against modern radiometric and astronomical calibration. It does not test his erosion-rate arithmetic of 1 inch per century on a 500-foot cliff. Modern geology also dates the Weald's denudation to the Cenozoic, so the claim's premise is not supported either.

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: The chart is the standard reference for numeric boundary ages. The fields used are the Cretaceous system, the Upper Cretaceous series, the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary age in Ma, and the base of the Cenomanian (the base of the Upper Cretaceous). The chart is downloadable as PDF and image, and ICS also provides a machine-readable version.
